newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu says no Hebron summit fixed as yet.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu says no Hebron summit fixed as yet.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday he and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had yet to fix a summit to sew up a deal giving self-rule to the West Bank town of Hebron.

Asked whether he would meet Arafat on Wednesday, Netanyahu said: "Possibly. We will see later. We haven't yet scheduled a meeting...We're still in the final steps of the conclusion of the Hebron negotiations."

The sides greeted the new year much the way they had spent the old one -- haggling over promised withdrawals and elusive peace deals. The handover of most of Hebron to the Palestinians has been delayed for nine months by Israeli security concerns.

"When I am satisfied that the basic conditions of security will have been reached, then we will sign it," Netanyahu told Israel Radio's English news. His spokesman Shai Bazak said on Wednesday that security issues were still in dispute.

U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy Dennis Ross scrambled to close a deal. Some 400 Israelis live and study in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs, drawn by the tomb of the biblical Abraham holy to Moslem and Jew alike.

"We're still working and I think there is a genuine desire to reach an agreement. So we are going to keep working and I hope we can reach it soon," Ross told reporters after meeting Netanyahu in Jerusalem and Arafat in Gaza on Tuesday.

Israeli and PLO officials had said earlier the leaders would probably meet on Wednesday when negotiators could initial the deal. But the two sides were still at odds over security, future withdrawals and the release of Palestinian prisoners.

Bazak said Israel was rejecting a Palestinian demand to join Israeli patrols near Abraham's tomb, was still insisting on tough security measures for the key Martyrs Street and wanted a ban on Palestinian police carrying rifles near Jewish enclaves.

The PLO views Israel's release of Palestinian prisoners as crucial to winning support for peace deals on the Palestinian street. Palestinians also demand target dates for future Israeli redeployments in West Bank rural areas.

Despite Netanyahu's opposition -- and that of right-wing cabinet members -- to swapping occupied Arab land for peace, the Likud party leader came to power vowing to uphold the accords with the PLO of the left-leaning government he ousted in May.
"Cabinet ministers can vote as they wish but I think that we have a responsibility and I am confident that we'll pass it in the cabinet," Netanyahu said.
"It was a very bad agreement that we received from the previous government but I think it's been vastly improved."

Jewish settlers in the town said they were praying for a miracle to prevent Israeli troops from pulling back and warned of impending bloodshed. They scuffled with Palestinians on Tuesday and tried to take over Arab houses in the casbah.
"I appeal even at this moment to the prime minister: Don't sign an agreement that will endanger our lives," Hebron settler leader Rabbi Moshe Levinger told Israel Radio on Wednesday.
Jewish settlers, who number 130,000 in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, helped Netanyahu sweep to power in elections last May on a promise to be tough with the Palestinians.
But Netanyahu has come under pressure from Washington, Israel's closest ally, to honour peace deals and withdraw from Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns due for self-rule.
In a message delivered by Ross, Clinton praised Netanyahu for "decisions which the prime minister made in order to advance the peace talks" and invited him to Washington.
